_comment: Curated, substantive intros for category and region browse pages, read by generate_pages.py. Where a key is absent the generator falls back to its auto-generated one-liner, so this can be filled in over time (counties are mostly left to the fallback for now). Keep these about genuine recurring traditions, motifs and landscape — not keyword padding. Keys: categories use the internal category id; regions use the region tag slug.

categories.beast: Britain and Ireland teem with monstrous beasts — the spectral black dogs of lonely lanes, the water-horses that drag riders down to drowning, and the territorial 'worms' and wild cattle of older belief. Many are bound to a single lake, moor or parish, where the creature guards a boundary or warns of a coming death.
categories.ghost: The ghosts of these islands are rarely vague. They are the wronged revenant who will not stay buried, the screaming skull that cannot be moved, the phantom coach, and the weeping or radiant figure tied to a named hall or churchyard — stories that preserve old anxieties about unquiet death, broken oaths and the boundary between the living and the dead.
categories.fairy: The fair folk of British and Irish tradition are neither tiny nor harmless: the Irish sídhe of the hollow hills, the Welsh Tylwyth Teg, the household brownies and boggarts, and the changelings left in a stolen child's place. Encounters turn on courtesy, theft, and time that runs strangely beneath the hill.
categories.water: Water holds its own people and its own perils — mermaids and selkies, the kelpie and each-uisge of the lochs, drowned bells and whole kingdoms sunk beneath the waves. These are the traditions of communities living by lake, river and a sea that both fed them and took them.
categories.dragon: The dragons of Britain and Ireland are usually earthbound and territorial: the wyrms and 'worms' of the north, the guardian coiled around a well or hoard, the red dragon of Welsh prophecy. Most are fixed to a named hill or village and a local hero whose slaying of the beast is still pointed out in the landscape.
categories.witch: From the trial records of North Berwick and Pendle to the cunning-folk and charmers of village life, the witch-lore of these islands mixes real persecution with belief in the evil eye, shape-shifting hares and butter that would not churn. Many places still carry the name of a woman who was accused, drowned or burned.
categories.deity: Older gods linger in the landscape — the Dagda and the Morrígan of Irish myth, Brigid and Lugh, the Brythonic figures of the Mabinogi, and the Romano-British deities of spring and grove. Their names survive in rivers, hills and holy wells long after their worship faded.
categories.giant: Giants are the great landscape-shapers of folk tradition: hurling the stones that became circles and causeways, gouging out valleys, and leaving their 'graves' and 'fingers' across the hills. Where ordinary people could not have raised a monument, the giants were said to have built it.
categories.location: Some places gathered folklore for thousands of years — stone circles said to be dancers turned to stone, holy wells sought for healing, barrows that must not be disturbed, and hills where a king and his knights are said to sleep. These are the sites where the supernatural was felt to press closest to the land.
categories.hero: The legendary figures of these islands range from Arthur and his knights to Fionn mac Cumhaill and the Fianna, from Robin Hood to the saints and outlaws whose deeds are still tied to named places. History and folklore blur: many were real, yet tradition gave them sleeping caves, buried treasure and returns foretold.
categories.pirate: Beyond the documented history, British and Irish coasts kept a folklore of pirates, privateers and wreckers — figures like Grace O'Malley and the smugglers of the Cornish and Essex shores, remembered in ballad and treasure-lore and in tales of false lights luring ships onto the rocks.

regions.england: English folklore is a patchwork of county traditions — the black dogs of East Anglia, the dragons and 'worms' of the north, the boggarts and witches of Lancashire, and the green men and well-dressings of the older calendar. Much of it is rooted in a single parish, stone or stretch of road.
regions.scotland: Scottish tradition runs from the Highland water-horses and the Cailleach who shapes the mountains to the selkies and trows of Orkney and Shetland, the brownies of the farm, and the witch trials of the Lowlands. Gaelic and Norse belief meet across its glens and islands.
regions.wales: Welsh folklore is steeped in the Mabinogi and the Arthurian past — the red dragon of Dinas Emrys, the lake maidens of the Tylwyth Teg, the fairy cattle of the mountains, and the Mari Lwyd of midwinter. So many of its tales are anchored to a named lake, hill or holy well.
regions.ireland: Irish tradition is dense with the Tuatha Dé Danann and the sídhe of the hollow hills, the banshee's warning, the holy wells and their saints, and the heroes of the Ulster and Fenian cycles — the supernatural mapped onto raths, cairns and the great prehistoric monuments of the Boyne.
regions.northern-ireland: The six northern counties share in the wider island's folklore — the sídhe and the banshee, holy wells and saints, the Giant's Causeway said to be built by Finn McCool — alongside their own local traditions of haunted ground, witches and the restless dead.
regions.isle-of-man: Manx folklore keeps creatures all its own — the Moddey Dhoo, the black dog of Peel Castle; the destructive buggane; the helpful fenodyree; and the fairies who must be greeted at the Fairy Bridge — in a tradition shaped by both Gaelic and Norse settlement.
regions.channel-islands: The folklore of the Channel Islands blends Norman-French and island tradition — witches and the sabbat, black dogs such as the Tchico, the fairy-haunted menhir of La Gran'mère du Chimquière, and the saints who gave the islands their names.
